questions.q: What does a security policy state, as distinct from a standard or procedure?
options: The what and why, at a level of abstraction that survives a change of vendor or technology stack
The exact product and token length a specific vendor must use
The literal click-by-click steps to configure a specific tool
A list of every auditor's test procedures for the current quarter
questions.explain: A policy states what the organization requires and why, deliberately leaving out vendor- or tool-specific detail so it doesn't need rewriting every time the technology changes.

questions.q: Why does changing a policy count as a governance event, unlike a routine procedure edit?
options: Because procedures are reviewed by the board, while policies are not
Because a policy is where the organization formally commits to a requirement and accepts accountability for it, approved at the executive/board level
Because policies are stored in a different file format
Because only procedures are subject to external audit
questions.explain: Policies are approved at the top because they represent a formal organizational commitment and accountability — changing one requires the same level of re-approval, which is why they change rarely.

questions.q: What does a standard add that a policy deliberately leaves out?
options: Board-level sponsorship
A statement of why the requirement exists at all
The team responsible for executing day-to-day tasks
Specific, measurable requirements that can actually be tested for compliance, such as "session timeout is 15 minutes of inactivity"
questions.explain: A standard translates a policy's "what and why" into something concrete enough for an auditor or automated control check to actually verify.

questions.q: What goes wrong when a standard is written with policy-level vagueness, such as "use strong authentication"?
options: The standard becomes too specific to apply to more than one vendor
It automatically becomes a procedure instead of a standard
It can't actually be audited, so compliance reporting against it turns into a judgment call instead of a measurement
It requires board approval that a specific standard would not
questions.explain: A standard needs to be specific and measurable enough for an auditor or control check to verify compliance. Vague, policy-level language makes that verification subjective instead of testable.

questions.q: Why do procedures change more often than standards or policies?
options: Because procedures require board re-approval for every edit
Because procedures are legally mandated to be rewritten annually
Because procedures are owned by security leadership rather than the executing team
Because procedures track the literal steps in a specific tool's current interface, which changes more frequently than the underlying requirement
questions.explain: Procedures are the step-by-step how-to for a specific tool, owned by the team that executes them — they track interface and tooling changes, which happen far more often than policy or standard changes.
